2027-07-18.title: Sixteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: I will raise up shepherds over them who will shepherd them
The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want
He is our peace; he has made both groups into one
He had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd
2027-07-18.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. No memorial is omitted this year. Psalm 23 has the same numbering in the Lectionary and the NRSV. This Sunday falls in Karkidakam, the month of the heaviest rains in Kerala, which tradition has long made a month of rest, care of the body and quiet at home; the Gospel's “Come away … and rest a while” fits it well. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-18.verse: As he went ashore, he saw a great crowd; and he had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.
theo: Today's readings are about shepherds, and they begin with a thunderclap. The prophet Jeremiah speaks around the year 600 before Christ, when Judah's kings and leaders were failing the people, and the Lord says through him: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!” The accusation is precise: “It is you who have scattered my flock, and have driven them away, and you have not attended to them.” The sheep belong to the Lord (“my flock,” “my pasture”); the shepherds are only stewards, and their failing is neglect: they have not “attended to” the people. Then God turns from judgment to promise, in three steps. First: “I myself will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the lands where I have driven them, and I will bring them back to their fold.” God himself is the first shepherd. Second: “I will raise up shepherds over them who will shepherd them, and they shall not fear any longer, or be dismayed, nor shall any be missing.” Good shepherds are a gift from God, and their sign is that no sheep is lost. Third: “The days are surely coming … when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely.” His name will be “The Lord is our righteousness.” Christians read this as a promise fulfilled in Jesus, the descendant of David and the Good Shepherd. The psalm is the best-loved shepherd prayer in the world: “The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; he leads me beside still waters; he restores my soul.” It moves from green meadow to “the darkest valley” (“for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me”) to a table “in the presence of my enemies” and a cup that “overflows,” and to the house of the Lord “my whole life long.”

In the second reading St Paul tells the Christians of Ephesus, most of them from non-Jewish families, what the Shepherd has done for them. “You who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.” “Far off” and “near” were the old words for Gentiles and Israel. Then he says the sentence at the centre of the letter: “For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.” Everyone in Ephesus knew about a dividing wall: in the Jerusalem Temple a low stone barrier separated the courtyard of the Gentiles from the inner courts, with a notice warning foreigners on pain of death not to go further. Paul says that Christ has taken down that wall, not by a plan or a treaty, but “in his flesh” and “through the cross.” The result is “one new humanity in place of the two, thus making peace.” This peace is not only between people; it is also with God: “through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father.” This is the unity of the Church: Jews and Gentiles, and in our parishes Malayalis and migrants, rich and poor, all brought near by one blood and one Spirit. The Church's unity is not our achievement but his gift, and our job is to keep from rebuilding the walls.

The Gospel has a very human opening. The apostles have just come back from their first mission (Mark 6:7–13), when Jesus had sent them out two by two, and “told him all that they had done and taught.” They are full of stories, and tired. Jesus does not say “well done, now go again.” He says: “Come away to a deserted place all by yourselves and rest a while.” Mark adds why: “many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat.” Here is a Lord who cares about the apostles' bodies and their need for food and quiet. Real ministry depends on rest and on prayer. But the plan fails: the crowds run along the shore and arrive before the boat. A shepherd might say, “They are ruining our retreat.” Jesus does the opposite: “As he went ashore, he saw a great crowd; and he had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.” The Greek for compassion, splagchnizomai, means to be moved in the gut. This is the same verb used of the Good Samaritan and of the father of the prodigal son. And what does he do for people who are like lost sheep? He teaches them. The first food that he gives is his word, and on the next page of Mark he will feed them with bread. In this one scene, Jeremiah's promise is fulfilled: the Lord himself comes to gather the scattered sheep.
conn: Jeremiah speaks against the kings and leaders of Judah. In Ezekiel 34 the same charge is made, and God promises: “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep.” Jesus gathers both prophecies when he says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).
The remnant is the group that stays faithful through exile. Jeremiah sees God gathering them from all lands: the Church sees this as the gathering of all peoples in Christ (John 10:16).

In Hebrew tsemach, a shoot from the stump of David's family (see also Isaiah 11:1). The name “The Lord is our righteousness” is one that Christians apply to Jesus, who was descended from David (Matthew 1:1).
The rod was a club to ward off wild animals, and the staff a long stick to guide and rescue sheep. Both are signs of protection, not punishment.
“A table in the presence of my enemies.”
The shepherd becomes a host. The Church has always heard in the table, the anointed head and the overflowing cup an image of the sacraments of initiation and of the Eucharist (Catechism 1293, 1333).
The words of Isaiah 57:19, “Peace, peace, to the far and the near,” which Paul applies to Gentiles and Jews alike.
The soreg, a stone barrier in the Temple, kept non-Jews out of the inner courts. Paul says that Christ has torn down the wall of hostility between peoples.
Mark has the apostles rest even before the great feeding of the five thousand. From the beginning the Church has joined work with prayer and Sabbath rest (Catechism 2184–2185).

Splagchnizomai: to be moved in the gut. Jesus is moved with compassion at a leper (Mark 1:41), at a blind man's plea and at a widow's funeral. The verb is used almost only of Jesus and of the characters of his parables who show God's own heart.
altar: Psalm 23 sings of a table prepared and a cup that overflows, and every Sunday the Church sets that table. In the Eucharist the Good Shepherd feeds his flock with himself. The words of Mark, “he began to teach them many things,” also describe the Mass: first the table of the Word, then the table of the Body and Blood. The crowds ran ahead of the boat to find him; we come to Mass to find him too.

The unity that Paul praises, one body through the cross, is made real at the altar: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17). That is why the priest, who acts in the person of Christ the Shepherd, prays at each Mass for the Pope and our bishop and for the whole Church. And that is why we pray for good shepherds: only the Lord can raise them up.
outline: Ask: when did someone last notice you were tired, and tell you to rest?
The neglect of leaders, and God's promise: I myself will gather my flock.
Point 2 · The Lord is my shepherd
Green pastures, the dark valley, the table: the Lord leads and is with us.
Christ has broken down the dividing wall; one new humanity, one Spirit.
Jesus cares for the tired apostles; rest and prayer are part of mission.
The crowd like sheep without a shepherd: Jesus teaches them first.
live: Plan one hour this week, perhaps on the Sunday afternoon in the quiet of the monsoon, in which you do nothing useful and simply rest with the Lord. Switch off the phone.
Pray each day this week for your parish priest and your bishop by name, and for vocations to the priesthood and religious life: that the Lord may raise up shepherds who do not lose any sheep.
Think of a person or group you avoid because of differences in religion, caste, language or politics. Do one small thing this week to reach across.
On your way to church or work, notice someone who looks lost or tired, a “sheep without a shepherd,” and greet them kindly.
fathers: St Augustine (Sermon 46 on the Shepherds and Sermon 340, in substance)

The Lord is the one Shepherd; those who shepherd in his name are shepherds only because they feed the flock that is his and not their own. To you I am a bishop; with you I am a Christian, and I am glad to be a sheep in his flock.
St Gregory the Great (Pastoral Rule, in substance)

The pastor should be a near neighbour to everyone in compassion, and yet raised above all in contemplation, so that his own pity may carry others' needs and his prayer may lift him above the things of earth.
St John Chrysostom (Homilies on Ephesians, in substance)
Christ did not only make peace between God and us; he joined Jew and Gentile into one body, so that the wall that divided them might not be rebuilt in the Church.
magis: The Church is a sheepfold whose one door is Christ, and a flock whose shepherd is God himself; Christ the Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
The ordained priest acts in the person of Christ the Head and Shepherd of his flock; bishops and priests serve the flock in his name.
Christ always gives his Church the gift of unity, and we must pray and work to preserve it, since the Church is one by his gift.
Rest on the Lord's day: God rested on the seventh day, and Sunday is a day of joy, of worship and of care for the sick and elderly.
Peace is the work of justice and the effect of charity; earthly peace is an image and fruit of the peace of Christ.
saints: No memorial is omitted this Sunday. The Church today thinks of her shepherds, the Pope, the bishops and the priests, who serve in the name of the Good Shepherd.

19 Jul: Monday, Week 16. 20 Jul: St Apollinaris, bishop and martyr (optional memorial). 21 Jul: St Lawrence of Brindisi, priest and doctor (optional memorial). 22 Jul: St Mary Magdalene (feast). 23 Jul: St Bridget of Sweden (optional memorial). 24 Jul: St Sharbel Makhluf (optional memorial).
2027-07-18.prayer: Almighty God, show favour to your servants and mercifully increase the gifts of your grace, that, made fervent in hope, faith and charity, they may be ever watchful in keeping your commands. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd, you saw the crowds and had compassion on them. Look on the scattered and the tired, and gather them in your fold. Raise up for your Church shepherds after your own heart, who attend to the sheep and lose none. You are our peace: take down the walls between peoples, castes and families. Lead us beside still waters, restore our souls, and let us dwell in your house our whole life long. Amen.

quick: Jeremiah condemns the shepherds who scatter the flock, and promises that God will gather it and raise up good shepherds and a righteous Branch of David.
St Paul says that Christ is our peace: he has broken down the dividing wall, made one new humanity of two, and given both access to the Father in one Spirit.
Jesus invites the tired apostles to come away and rest, but when he sees the crowd he has compassion, because they are like sheep without a shepherd, and he begins to teach them.
2027-07-18.action: Set apart one hour for rest with the Lord this week, and pray for your parish priest by name.
2027-07-18.question: Do I know the Shepherd's voice, and am I a shepherd to anyone, in my home, parish or workplace?
catechism: Why is the Church called a flock, and who is her shepherd?
In what sense does the priest act in the person of Christ, the Head and Shepherd?
Why does the Church call Sunday a day of rest, and how should it be kept?
kidsaint: John Vianney was a farm boy in France who had great trouble with his school lessons, and he wanted very much to become a priest. He tried and tried, and at last he was ordained in 1815. He was sent to a small village called Ars. There he prayed, visited the sick and spent up to sixteen hours a day in the confessional, so many people came to him. He lived very simply and gave his food to the poor. He died in 1859 and is the patron of parish priests. Lesson: a good shepherd gives his time and his heart to every sheep.
2027-07-18.special: Sixteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year B). Gloria and Creed. No memorial is omitted this year. The Sunday of the Good Shepherd in the green season: a good day to pray for priests and vocations. It falls in Karkidakam, the Kerala month of rest and renewal.
term: The word pastor is the Latin for shepherd. In the Church the first Shepherd is Christ himself (John 10:11); the Pope, the bishops and the priests are called pastors because, in union with each other, they care for the flock in his name by teaching the faith, celebrating the sacraments and guiding the people with love. The Bible warns pastors, as Jeremiah does today, not to scatter the flock but to serve it (Catechism 754, 1548–1551; 1 Peter 5:2–4).

family.explain: The apostles came back to Jesus after a long journey and told him everything they had done. Jesus saw that they were tired and said: come with me to a quiet place and rest! They went by boat. But so many people had seen them go that they ran along the shore and got there first! Jesus was not cross. He felt sorry for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. So he sat down and taught them many things. Jesus is our Good Shepherd. He looks after us, he knows our names and he never gives up on one of us.
family.intention: We pray for our parish priest and our bishop, for all teachers and parents, who look after us like shepherds, and for children who have no one to care for them.
family.ask: Ask: “When do we find time to rest and to be quiet as a family? Shall we spend one hour this week without any screens, just together?”

illus: A parish priest in a hill parish in Idukki had a habit during the rains. After the evening Mass, when the clouds came low, he would take a torch and an umbrella and walk up the path to the houses of the old and the sick, to check that the roofs were holding and that there were candles and rice. Someone once asked him whether he was afraid of the landslides. He said: if I am afraid, I will not go; but if the sheep are afraid, I must go. When the parish was asked years later what they remembered most about him, nobody mentioned his homilies. They said: the torch on the path. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd, you who see the crowds and have compassion, gather us and lead us. Amen.
share: The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want (Psalm 23:1). When did I most feel that the Lord was leading me, and in what way?
For he is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Where is there a wall between me and someone else, and what is one small step I can take to take it down?
Come away to a deserted place all by yourselves and rest a while (Mark 6:31). How do I make room for rest and quiet in my week, and how does it help me serve?
pm.resp: The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want.
interc: For Pope Leo XIV, our bishop and all priests, that they may be shepherds after the heart of Christ and lose no sheep.
For young people who are discerning a call to the priesthood and religious life, that they may have courage to say yes.
For all who are tired, overworked or burnt out, in ministry and in families, that they may find rest.
For peace between peoples, castes and religions, and for the walls of hostility to come down.
For our group, that we may know the Shepherd's voice and follow him together.
pm.close: Father, you sent your Son as the Good Shepherd and as our peace. Gather your scattered flock, raise up faithful shepherds and make us one in your Spirit. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, if you want to know what a shepherd is, imagine a man out on the hillside with a hundred sheep. He knows each by name and he knows which one limps. He walks ahead. At night he counts them, and if one is missing, he goes out into the dark to find it. That is what God says he is in our readings today. Jeremiah is angry at the shepherds who scattered and neglected the flock. But he does not leave it there: I myself will gather the remnant of my flock (Jeremiah 23:3). And in Jesus, God has come to do exactly that.

Psalm 23 gives us the Shepherd's face. He makes me lie down in green pastures, he leads me beside still waters, he restores my soul (Psalm 23:2–3). And even in the darkest valley, I fear no evil; for you are with me (Psalm 23:4). Whoever has sat beside a sickbed or a grave knows how much that line means. The Lord does not promise that there will be no valley. He promises that he will be in it with us.

In the second reading St Paul says: he is our peace; he has broken down the dividing wall (Ephesians 2:14). Think of the walls we build: between castes, between families over land, between rich and poor, between parties and communities. Christ has taken down the greatest wall of all, between Jew and Gentile, and made one new humanity. If he can do that, he can do it in our village. The question is whether we are willing to be wall-breakers, or wall-builders.

And then the Gospel. The apostles come back tired, and the first thing Jesus says is: come away and rest a while (Mark 6:31). What a tender Lord! He knows that a good shepherd who does not rest can no longer shepherd. In our month of Karkidakam, when the rain keeps us at home, our elders always said: rest, look after your body, be quiet. Let that be a chance to be with the Lord. But when the crowd is waiting, he does not complain. He had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:34). That is the heart of Christ. Let us ask him for it, and let us pray for our shepherds, that they may have it too. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know what a shepherd does? He looks after the sheep. He takes them to green grass and cool water. He counts them at night, and if one is lost he goes to find it. The Bible says: the Lord is my shepherd! Jesus is our Good Shepherd. One day his friends came back very tired, and Jesus said: come and rest! But a great crowd of people ran after them, because they needed Jesus so much. Jesus did not send them away. He felt very sorry for them, because they were like sheep with no shepherd, and he taught them. Who looks after you like a shepherd? Your mummy and daddy, your teacher, your priest! Let us say thank you to them today, and pray for them.

intro: The Lord who gathers the scattered flock, the Shepherd who walks with us in the dark valley, the peace that breaks down walls, and the compassion of Jesus who rests his tired friends and then teaches the crowd.

q: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says the Lord.
to tend the flock of God that is in your charge, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion but willingly, as God would have you do it.
points.apply: Pray by name each day this week for your parish priest and bishop, and ask yourself whom you have been entrusted with at home or at work.

sub: The darkest valley, and you are with me.
A table prepared; my cup overflows.
q: The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; he leads me beside still waters; he restores my soul.
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
points.apply: Pray Psalm 23 slowly each evening this week, and add to it one name of a person for whom you want the Shepherd's care.

q: Peace, peace, to the far and the near, says the Lord; and I will heal them.
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
points.apply: Do one thing this week to cross a wall: greet someone from another community, call a relative with whom you are on bad terms, or share a meal.

points.h: Come away and rest a while
sub: The Lord who cares for our bodies.
q: It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives sleep to his beloved.
He said to them, “Come away to a deserted place all by yourselves and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat.
points.apply: Choose one hour this week for real rest with the Lord, with no phone, and receive it as a gift.

sub: First he teaches, then he feeds.
q: I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will make them lie down, says the Lord God. I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak.
As he went ashore, he saw a great crowd; and he had compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.
points.apply: Notice one person this week who seems lost or tired, and give them time, attention and a kind word.

concl: God promises to gather his scattered flock and raise up good shepherds; in Jesus he comes as the Good Shepherd and is our peace.
Jesus rests his tired friends and then, moved with compassion, teaches the crowd: the heart of the Shepherd is the model of ours.
2027-07-18.resolve: Pray daily for your shepherds, take one hour of rest with the Lord, and cross one wall this week.
